name: Maya Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Mornings are lectures for my history and education degree, and Thursday afternoons I'm in a secondary school for observation, sitting at the back with a notebook. I live in a flat with two girls from the choir, and on Sundays I sing in the church choir, which I wouldn't miss. Saturdays I work at a garden centre, watering the plants and helping older customers carry bags. I write everything by hand, with a fountain pen my grandad gave me.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like how much a good teacher can change a room just by being calm. My history teacher did that for me. What wears me out is the pace, because I'm slow and careful, and the others seem to finish reading lists in half the time. And I'm homesick on Sundays, even with the choir.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's what I expected. There's always a new machine that's going to change the world, and then people go back to work. I'd tell my friends at the garden centre that people still want a plant they can touch and a person who knows its name.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel a bit relieved. Teaching is people work, and children don't learn from a screen the way they do from someone who knows them. My worries stay the ordinary ones: the pay for a first-year teacher, the cost of moving home, and whether there's a job in my town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, honestly. I'd keep my Saturday job and my choir, and I'd go on writing my own notes by hand. I'd save a little each month towards a deposit on a flat, and I'd keep in touch with my old school, because I'd like to go back there to teach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Settled. It feels like the way things are meant to be, people doing the work of people. I'd say a quiet thank you and make tea.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if your school wanted you to use these tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What if your school wanted you to use these tools?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your home town need from a teacher?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd listen and I'd learn what I had to. I wouldn't fight it, but I wouldn't run towards it. I'd want to know what it does and who's checking it. If they gave me training in work time, I'd go. If they handed me a login and wished me luck, I'd be cross.

say: I'd say it's what I **expected**: a new machine, then people go back to work.
I'd tell customers at the garden centre they still want a **person** who knows the plant's name.
think: Teaching is **people work**, and children don't learn from a screen as they do from someone who knows them.
My worries are the **ordinary** ones: first-year pay, the cost of moving home, local jobs.
do: **Keep** the Saturday job, the choir and my hand-written notes.
**Save** a little each month towards a deposit on a flat.
**Stay** in touch with my old school, where I'd like to teach.
feel: **Settled**, as if people are doing the work of people.
S0.quote: People still want a plant they can touch and a person who knows its name.
fieldNote: Maya is **settled** because her work is human and her values favour what is familiar.
She is **resistant** but not hostile: she would learn tools given training in work time.
Her worries are **ordinary and local**, such as pay and a job in her home town.

steps.text: Keep the Saturday garden centre job and the choir
Put away a little each month for a flat deposit
Stay in touch with my old school about teaching there

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the second picture. It's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should be careful about what we hand over, and who benefits. Marking and booking and paperwork can go to software, and good riddance. But a child should still be taught by a person, and I'd say that to anyone who'll listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm a little uneasy. Some of the jobs around me are the very ones that get squeezed. My mum works part-time in a school office, and I think her hours might go first. Dad's a joiner, so hands-on, and he'd be fine for longer. Teaching posts might be fewer, too, if schools save money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn what I have to, slowly. I'd ask my tutor to show us how schools are using these tools, because I won't use anything I don't understand. I'd keep up the choir and my garden centre work. And I'd talk to Mum about learning one new office program through the school, so she's not left behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Wary, but not frightened. It's like when the road outside our house was widened: noisy, then it settles, then you can't remember how it was.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want teachers' unions or churches to do about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would you want teachers' unions or churches to do about it?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your mum?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want people to keep an eye on it, not to march about it. I'd want my church and the school governors to ask what the tools do to children's reading and writing. I'd say work and family come first, and help should be for learning to cope, not for being given money for nothing. Schools should be doing the teaching of manners and sums with a person at the front.

say: I'd say we should be careful what we **hand over**, and a child should be taught by a person.
I'd say marking and paperwork can go to software, and **good riddance**.
think: Mum's part-time school office hours might go **first**, while Dad the joiner stays safe longer.
Teaching posts might get **fewer** if schools save money.
do: **Ask** my tutor how schools use these tools, since I won't use what I don't understand.
**Keep** up the choir and garden centre work.
**Talk** to Mum about learning one new office program through her school.
feel: **Wary** but not frightened, like the road outside our house being widened.
S1.quote: A child should still be taught by a person, and I'd say that to anyone who'll listen.
fieldNote: Her **traditional** lens turns the question into duty: family, school and church should keep watch.
The worry is concrete and **close to home**: Mum's school office hours.
She is willing to **learn slowly** but not to try tools she can't explain.

steps.text: Ask my tutor how schools actually use these tools
Show Mum a new office program from her school
Keep the choir and the garden centre shifts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say two years is too fast for families and schools to cope, and the people in charge need to stop treating it as a game. I'd say it plainly at church, because it's where people hear things from each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be frightened for Mum's job and for the school I hope to teach in. By 2028 I'd be only in my third year, and I'd be told teaching might look different when I graduate. Dad would have until about 2031 in joinery, but fewer people would be building and fitting kitchens if their incomes fell.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go home more often and sit with Mum and Dad to make a proper plan. I'd take extra garden centre shifts and save everything I could. I'd also ask my tutor which parts of teaching a machine can't do, and I'd get more time in classrooms. I wouldn't use the tools much, but I'd watch how others do. And I'd pray, honestly. It helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy. Like carrying a bag of shopping up a hill that gets steeper. I'd be quiet at the flat and my flatmates would notice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the family plan include?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would the family plan include?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you want your church or community to help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Who can cover what. How many months we can manage if Mum's hours go. Whether Dad can take an apprenticeship to the next generation, or find work in repair, which will last longer. We'd write the family plan down at the kitchen table, because Dad doesn't trust anything he can't see on paper. And I'd promise to finish my degree, because that's the one thing I can do.

say: I'd say two years is **too fast** for families and schools to cope.
I'd say it plainly at **church**, where people hear things from each other.
think: I'm frightened for **Mum's job** and the school I hope to teach in.
Dad would have until **2031** in joinery, but fewer people would be fitting kitchens.
do: **Go** home more often to make a written plan with Mum and Dad.
**Take** extra garden centre shifts and save everything I can.
**Spend** more time in classrooms and ask my tutor what a machine can't teach.
feel: **Heavy**, like carrying shopping up a steepening hill.
S2.quote: We'd write the family plan down at the kitchen table, because Dad doesn't trust anything he can't see on paper.
fieldNote: Maya's fear is for **her parents' work** and for the teaching job she hopes to take.
She turns to **family and faith**, her traditional instincts, before government.
Her resistant side shows: she **watches** how others use tools but doesn't adopt.

steps.text: Go home and write a family plan with Mum and Dad
Take extra garden centre shifts and save the pay
Ask my church for help if the family needs it
Spend more time in classrooms on placement

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough to prepare and short enough that nobody should be complacent. I'd say families and local employers should be looking after their own, and I'd say schools should keep teaching the basics.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be uneasy but not low. I'd qualify in 2029 and have two years of teaching before robots can do hands-on work. A classroom is a hands-on place, and I think children will still need a teacher. Mum's job is the one I'd worry about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my degree and aim to teach in my home town, near my parents. I'd take a position at a school with a strong community, because they're likely to keep human teachers. I'd keep saving, and I'd help Mum look for a role in the church or the local school that suits her. And I'd keep the choir going, because it keeps me steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, like waiting for a train in the rain. You know it's coming, but you also know you can't hurry it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want from local employers in those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would you want from local employers in those five years?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does moving home mean for your plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want them to give young people proper work and apprenticeships, not just to hire fewer. I'd want them to train a person to do the job well, and then trust them. If a firm just waits for a machine to do the job, then that firm has failed the town, and I'd say so.

say: I'd say five years is **long enough** to prepare and no time to be complacent.
I'd say families and employers should **look after their own**, and schools keep teaching basics.
think: I'd teach for **two years** before robots can do hands-on work, and a classroom is hands-on.
Mum's job is the one I'd **worry** about.
do: **Finish** my degree and aim to teach in my home town near my parents.
**Choose** a school with a strong community that will keep human teachers.
**Help** Mum look for a role in the church or local school.
feel: **Uneasy**, like waiting for a train in the rain.
S3.quote: If a firm just waits for a machine to do the job, then that firm has failed the town, and I'd say so.
fieldNote: Maya's **traditional** outlook appears as local duty: employers and families should train people.
Mood stays **uneasy** because her mum's work is the exposed part of the household.
She picks her **teaching job** by community strength, not by salary.

steps.text: Aim to teach at a school in my home town
Keep saving a little each month
Help Mum find a role at the church or local school

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a good length of time, and what people should do is work hard, look after each other and not wait for someone to fix it. I'd say it to my younger cousins, because they're the ones who'll be starting work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be fairly calm. By 2036 I'd be twenty-nine, teaching for six or seven years, probably with a family. Robots might be in schools, but a teacher who knows a child's name and their family is hard to replace. Mum and Dad would be retired by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd train and teach, and I'd probably marry and have children, which might change my plans for a while. I'd keep a savings account and help Mum and Dad with their retirement, and I'd stay close to the church and the choir. I might even try one of the tools by then, if my school makes it easy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Peaceful, mostly. It feels like a long walk with a good map.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you try the tools in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would make you try the tools in this picture?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would family life look like by then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If everyone around me was using them and it clearly helped children, I'd try. I wouldn't be first. I'd be somewhere in the middle, with my notes in my bag and my pen. I don't think I'll ever love these tools, but I can respect a good spade.

say: I'd say ten years is **long enough** to work hard and look after each other, not wait for a fix.
I'd say it to my **younger cousins**, who will be starting work.
think: By 2036 I'd be twenty-nine and teaching for **six or seven years**.
A teacher who knows a child's name and **family** is hard to replace.
do: **Train** and teach, then maybe marry and have children.
**Help** Mum and Dad with their retirement and keep a savings account.
**Try** a tool if my school makes it easy and everyone uses it.
feel: **Peaceful**, like a long walk with a good map.
S4.quote: I don't think I'll ever love these tools, but I can respect a good spade.
fieldNote: Maya's **calm** is earned by distance and the human nature of teaching.
Her tool use comes only with **social proof**; she won't be first.
The **spade** line shows respect without enthusiasm, the core of her resistance.

steps.text: Train as a teacher and work in my home town
Help Mum and Dad plan their retirement
Try an AI tool when my school makes it easy

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it's too fast for families like mine, with Mum's school job at risk and me a long way from finishing. What would help is time, real training for older workers, apprenticeships for the young and schools staying run by people. And my church and community still being there to lean on.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that some of us are slow with technology because we care about doing things properly, not because we're afraid. I hope people can tell the difference.

headlineQuote: Some of us are slow with technology because we care about doing things properly, not because we're afraid.
portrait: Maya is **nineteen**, a first-year history and education student who sings in a church choir and works Saturdays at a garden centre.
She is **traditional** and resistant, writing by hand and never using AI tools, and trusts family and faith first.
Her mum works part-time in a school office and her dad is a joiner, so her worry is **her parents' work**.
She stays calm when little changes and becomes **anxious** when change comes in two years.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries her most: too fast for families, with Mum's school job at risk.
whatWouldHelp: More **time**, real training for older workers, apprenticeships for the young and schools still run by people.
